title: Inventory and Glasshouse
premise: Rosalind Zhou, a literary translator in her forties, has spent decades erasing herself between languages while her mother's Shanghainese fades from her memory word by word. When the family glasshouse—her late mother's nursery and the site of an unspoken betrayal involving Rosalind's uncle—is listed for auction, she returns to catalog its contents and instead begins cataloging what was never said. As bidding war looms and her uncle's heirs press their claim, Rosalind must finally translate the sentence her mother spoke on her deathbed: that she chose silence to protect Rosalind, not herself. The novel ends with Rosalind letting the glasshouse go, keeping only a single pane of glass and the translated truth, speaking her mother's language aloud for the first time in years at the auction's close.
about_author: R. M. Okafor is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between Lagos, Manchester, and Singapore, and writes about the quiet violence of translation. Their short fiction has appeared in several small journals; Inventory and Glasshouse is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Rosalind, in third person limited POV, loses another Shanghainese word mid-translation at work and covers it with a French substitute no one notices. At home she maintains her literal inventory notebook of unsaid things. Emotional beat: the ache of erosion—the self thinning along with the language.

chapters.title: Notice of Sale
chapters.summary: A solicitor's letter arrives: the family glasshouse and land are up for auction, claimed by her uncle Wei's estate. Rosalind's POV reveals she hasn't been back in nineteen years. Her partner Daniel urges her to ignore it. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into reluctant obligation.

chapters.title: What the Glass Remembers
chapters.summary: Rosalind travels north to inventory the property for the auction house. In her mother's potting shed she finds a ledger written half in Shanghainese, entries stopping abruptly the year Rosalind left home. POV stays with Rosalind. Emotional beat: the past becoming physical, tactile, unavoidable.

chapters.title: Uncle Wei's Heirs
chapters.summary: Cousin Jun arrives with documents asserting full ownership and a buyer already interested. Flashbacks, woven into Rosalind's POV, show Uncle Wei's generosity that always carried a price. Rosalind signs nothing. Emotional beat: the first open collision over inheritance and history.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Rosalind catalogs the glasshouse object by object, each item triggering a memory she records in her unsaid-things notebook alongside the auction inventory. She discovers the ledger's final entry names her, not Wei. Emotional beat: mounting suspicion that her exile was arranged, not chosen.

chapters.title: The Interpreter's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Back in London, a client asks Rosalind to soften a testimony that would implicate a friend; she refuses and loses the contract. Parallel structure mirrors her childhood realization that her mother once interpreted—and altered—for Wei. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth pulling apart inside her.

chapters.title: Jun's Version
chapters.summary: Jun, in a rare shift to his first-person voice, admits his father died believing Rosalind had betrayed the family, and shows him a letter proving otherwise—a letter his father kept hidden. Emotional beat: revelation reframing everything; grief arriving before understanding.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Rosalind deciphers the ledger's last line: her mother confessed she let Wei believe the lie so Rosalind could leave freely, trading her own name for her daughter's escape. Rosalind attempts seventeen translations and keeps none. Emotional beat: climax of meaning—the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Going Once
chapters.summary: At the auction, Jun unexpectedly withdraws the claim, having read the ledger Rosalind left in the shed. The glasshouse sells to strangers. Rosalind, POV hers, stands silent as the gavel falls, holding one salvaged pane. Emotional beat: release entangled with loss.

chapters.title: Speaking It Aloud
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Rosalind installs the pane in her London window and plants her mother's camellia cutting beneath it. She reads the translated sentence aloud—in Shanghainese—to Daniel, then writes it into the inventory and crosses it out. Emotional beat: resolution through speech; the language saved by being given away.
